doc.title: Peter Appleyard interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, October 4, 2012

title: Working at the Colonial Tavern and befriending Ellington and other stars
summary: At Toronto's Colonial Tavern he met visiting greats; he recalls Duke Ellington and Harry Carney in New York much later.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: But during the time of the war, the Russians at the beginning were our enemies of course, as you remember. Then they came around to our side after Hitler invaded them. And all of a sudden I found myself playing in a Communist meeting one night. You know, and this drummer, who I had no idea was a Communist, he said, “You’ve got to play this gig for these people I’m in this group with.” I said, “yeah?” We go there and there’s a big Russian flag. But anyway I mean the war was — they were on our side, and we had Russian prisoners in my town, and they let them all out, and they would gather in the streets and sing, a cappella, oh it was so beautiful, some of these voices. But that was the war. But that was the story about the guy — yeah they took him right — and they didn’t even let him take his clothes. He left the bass on the stand and took him out and put him on an airplane right away. Yeah. But it was great. And then of course I came back and before I left England I had a job at a place called the Isle of Wight. And all the liners would go by there, heading for New York. And I’d sit on the beach looking at these boats and think oh God, if I could only get on one of those, as a gig, you know, so I could go to New York. And here I am all of a sudden, a job in Bermuda with a stop off in New York which was great. Then, after I got my union card I left the shop selling ties and shirts, and I got a job in the Colonial Tavern where I saw Red. It was two levels. We were on the bottom level, and the big shots were on the second level. Everyone came. Duke — oh gosh, every major star — Tatum, Billie Holiday, the Basie band, the Hampton band, and I got to know them all. Because in their break they’d come downstairs and have a taste and listen to us you see. And if the band came in they’d always do two weeks. And so what

we would do is to have a weenie roast or whatever, spaghetti night, and invite them all over. So the room was filled with Ray Nance, Clark Terry, Duke Ellington, and I mean Duke, I knew him intimately as I know you basically now. The last time I saw him I was with Benny at the Rainbow Grill at Rockefeller Center, and I went to the Stage Delicatessen and Harry Carney, the baritone player, was sitting there: “Hey Peter, how are you.” I said, “Harry, how are you?” He said, “What are you doing working here?” I said, “Yeah I’m with Goodman.” He said, “Oh great.” I said, “Are you working with Duke tonight?” Because he had a nice shirt on. And he said, “Yeah.” I said, “How is he?” He said, “He’s right over there at the takeout counter.” And Duke lived upstairs and he was an ice cream junkie. He was standing at the takeout counter with a robe on it looked like he had since 1917. No socks on. Slippers. In this sophisticated restaurant in the middle of New York. And he turned around and saw me and he said, “Ahh, Mr. Appleyard” and gave me —

So that was fortunate working at The Colonial. Because everyone worked there, all the greats, and I can’t even remember — Artie Shaw came. Goodman didn’t come while I was there but oh, I can’t remember, Erroll Garner, everybody.
So you got to know them as personalities as well as musicians.
You know, how to behave, how to carry yourself?
